lessons.culture: In many Gulf homes shoes come off at the door, and the host often serves coffee and dates before anything else. In traditional families the majlis (guest room) may receive men and women separately, so the host tells you where to go. "7ayyaak allah" is the warm everyday way to welcome someone.

exercises.prompt: You arrive and the host says: "حياك الله". Reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct and kind, but it answers a spoken salaam, not the welcome "7ayyaak allah".

exercises.tip: The set answer to "7ayyaak allah" is "allah y7ayyiik".

exercises.prompt: The host says: "شرفتونا". Reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct Modern Standard Arabic, but heavy for a doorway.

exercises.tip: A short reply is warmest: "the honor is ours".

lessons.culture: In the Gulf, Arabic coffee (gahwa) is poured in small cups without sugar, usually with dates or sweets, and the host serves the guest first. To say you have had enough, gently shake the empty cup from side to side. "Khudh raa7tak" and "il-beet beetak" tell a guest to relax completely. "What" is "shnu" in Kuwait and "shu" in the UAE.

lessons.culture: Meals are often served on a sufra (a spread laid on the floor or a big table), and guests eat with the right hand or a spoon. A Gulf host will press you to take more more than once, so a polite "shabi3naa, al-7amdu lillah" is the honest way to say you are full. "Bil-3aafya" is said to people who are eating, and "tislam iidik" thanks the cook.

lessons.culture: Guests in the Gulf are pressed to stay longer, so leaving takes a few rounds of "maa nagbal a3dhaar" and polite refusals. In many homes the host passes around an incense burner (mabkhara) with oud at the end, which signals the visit is ending, and the guest wafts the smoke toward themselves. "Fii amaan allah" is the standard goodbye, and "inshaa allah" is used for anything about the future.

exercises.prompt: You say "سلملي على الأهل". The host replies. What?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal; the spoken answer is just "yuusal".

exercises.tip: "yuusal" means "it will arrive", i.e. it will be passed on.

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you "تصبح على خير". Reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but generic; the usual reply is "w inta min ahla" (and you are among its people).

exercises.tip: To a woman say "tisba7iin 3ala khayr", to several people "tisba7uun 3ala khayr".

challenge.title: Hosting or Visiting: A Full Exchange
challenge.instructions: Write a short conversation where you either welcome a guest into your home from the door to the table, or visit someone else's home and take your leave at the end. Use at least one greeting-at-the-door phrase, one phrase about food or drink, and one closing or thanking phrase.
required_elements: a welcome phrase at the door (e.g. 7ayyaak allah / tfaddal daakhil)
an offer of food or drink (e.g. gahwa willa shaay?)
a closing thanks or goodbye (e.g. y3tiik il-3aafya / fii amaan allah)
